idiom_name: using statement / using declaration over IDisposable.Dispose() (await using + IAsyncDisposable for asynchronous teardown)
implementation_notes: The runtime keeps the classic owner structure - a class implementing IDisposable with an idempotent Dispose(), ideally via the dispose pattern - but callers never write the try/finally: using (var r = Open()) { ... } and the C# 8 using var r = Open(); declaration compile to a finally clause that calls Dispose() on every exit path, and await using does the same for IAsyncDisposable. What replaces the C++ destructor is that compiler-emitted finally plus the interface contract, so the release point is the end of the enclosing block; the finalizer slot and GC.SuppressFinalize exist only as a safety net for handles the programmer forgot, because collection time is unpredictable and the recommended shape forwards the finalizer to the same Dispose(bool) the using path uses.
pitfalls: GC-timing cleanup is not RAII: relying on the finalizer (or on the GC in general) to release a lease, lock or connection makes the release time unpredictable under memory pressure and can starve a pool; always release through using/Dispose.
A Dispose() that throws or blocks moves a hidden failure to an unrelated statement: keep it non-throwing, and give callers an explicit Commit/Flush/Close that surfaces the errors they must act on.

Because the release point is implicit, any reference that escapes the using block (closure, event handler, cache) is used after disposal and fails later with ObjectDisposedException instead of at the misuse.
